title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, Planetary Transits Across the Sun (transit index page)
note: Read in full (curl, page dated 2026 Aug 06 in its footer). Source of the 13 Mercury transits per century, the May 8 and November 10 dates, the 7, 13 and 33 year November intervals, the 8, 121.5, 8, 105.5 year Venus pattern, the 1901 to 2050 and 1601 to 2400 tables with minimum separations, the 1999 graze label, and the statement that predictions use algorithms from the Explanatory Supplement (1974) and Meeus (1989).

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, Seven Century Catalog of Mercury Transits: 1601 CE to 2300 CE
note: Read in full (curl). 94 transits, 31 in May at the descending node and 63 in November at the ascending node; the 13, 33 and 46 year commensurabilities with their residuals in days; the 46-year series; the full table of contacts, minimum separations and series; the 1937 May 11 row with no interior contacts; and the statement that Besselian elements come from Meeus's Transits (1989).

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, Six Millennium Catalog of Venus Transits: 2000 BCE to 4000 CE
note: Read in full (curl). 81 transits, 44 in June and 37 in December; the 8-year resonance with the 2.45 day shortfall; the 243-year series of 88,756 days; node dates drifting from about May 21 and November 19 five thousand years ago; rows with missing contacts such as -1763 and -0540; elements from Meeus (1989).

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, Key to Catalog of Transits
note: Read in full (curl). Column definitions, contact definitions, the 46-year (16,802 day) and 243-year (88,757 day) series, and the ΔT recipe: Stephenson 1997 before 1600, observed values 1600 to the present, extrapolation for the future.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, Transit visibility (Calculating the Sun's Altitude and Azimuth)
note: Read in full (curl). The geocentric visibility formulas, the 2004 June 8 catalogue row with 626.9 arcseconds minimum separation, and the stated error of the geocentric approximation: up to 3 minutes of time for Mercury and 10 minutes for Venus.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, 1999 Transit of Mercury (Observer's Handbook article)
note: Read in full (curl). Geocentric contacts and position angles for the 1999 November 15 grazing transit, the convergence of contacts II and III near the southern limit, and the JPL DE200 ephemeris.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, The 2004 Transit of Venus (Observer's Handbook 2004)
note: Read (curl, text extracted). Geocentric contacts 05:13:29, 05:32:55, 08:19:44, 11:06:33, 11:25:59 UT with position angles, and the up to 30 arcsecond parallax shift of Venus.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, 2006 Transit of Mercury (Observer's Handbook 2006)
note: Read (curl, text extracted). Geocentric contacts for 2006 November 8 to 9, the up to 13 arcsecond parallax shift of Mercury and the up to one minute local difference.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, The 2012 Transit of Venus (Observer's Handbook 2012)
note: Read in full (curl). Geocentric contacts 22:09:38, 22:27:34, 01:29:36, 04:31:39, 04:49:35 UT with position angles, the plus or minus 7 minute local spread, the black-drop description, VSOP87 ephemerides and the Meeus (1989) and Explanatory Supplement (1974) algorithms.

title: Espenak, F., NASA GSFC, 2004 and 2012 Transits of Venus (poster text, 2002)
note: Read in full (curl). Relative motion of about 4 arcminutes per hour, semidiameters of 29 and 945 arcseconds, the 30 arcsecond parallax and plus or minus 7 minute topocentric correction, and the remark that seeing and diffraction make Halley's timings impractical.

title: Espenak, F., EclipseWise, Transits of Mercury and Venus
note: Read through a fetch summary (the site blocks scripted downloads). States that ephemerides come from JPL DE430 and DE431, cites the 2018 Six Millennium Canon of Transits, and names the Explanatory Supplement (1974) and Meeus (1989) as the algorithm sources. No ΔT model or semidiameters are stated.

title: Espenak, F., EclipseWise, 2016 Transit of Mercury (Observer's Handbook article)
note: Read through a fetch summary with quoted table values. Geocentric contacts 11:12:19, 11:15:31, 14:57:26, 18:39:14, 18:42:26 UT1 with position angles 83.2, 83.5, 153.8, 224.1 and 224.4 degrees, minimum separation 318.5 arcseconds, JPL DE406.

title: Espenak, F., EclipseWise, 2019 Transit of Mercury (Observer's Handbook article)
note: Read through a fetch summary with quoted table values. Geocentric contacts 12:35:27, 12:37:08, 15:19:48, 18:02:33, 18:04:14 UT1 with position angles, minimum separation 75.9 arcseconds, JPL DE406, local times differing by up to 2 minutes, and the remark that the thread-breaking time is delayed by some seconds, up to a minute.

title: Espenak, F. (2018) Six Millennium Canon of Transits: -1999 to +4000, Astropixels Publishing, Portal, AZ
note: Not read. Known from the EclipseWise transit index, which cites it. Its constants, ΔT model and transit counts were not seen.

title: Meeus, J. (1989) Transits, Willmann-Bell, Richmond
note: Not read. Cited by Espenak as the source of the Besselian elements and algorithms behind the NASA transit catalogues, and by Meeus's Astronomical Algorithms as the place for transit elements and formulae.

title: Institute of Applied Astronomy RAS, Astronomical Yearbook 2016: Transit of Mercury of 2016 May 9
note: Read in full (curl). Elements at conjunction in right ascension, geocentric phases with position angles and sub-planet points, the four local-circumstance formulas T = T0 + a r sin f' + b r cos f' cos(c + l), and a table of Russian cities. Ephemeris not stated in the file.

title: Institute of Applied Astronomy RAS, Astronomical Yearbook 2019: Transit of Mercury of 2019 November 11
note: Read in full (curl). Same layout as 2016, with TDT - UT1 = 70.0 s stated, geocentric contacts 12:35:26.3, 12:37:07.7, 15:19:47.3, 18:02:32.1, 18:04:13.5 UT and the four reduction formulas.

title: ESO and IMCCE, VT-2004 Observing Campaign Results
note: Read in full (curl). 4550 contact timings from 1510 observers, the final AU of 149 608 708 plus or minus 11 835 km, and the alternative solution for the radii of the Sun (695 980.7 plus or minus 806 km) and Venus (6052.3 plus or minus 7.0 km).

title: Rocher, P. and Arlot, J.-E. (IMCCE) (2004) Analysis of the Observations of Contacts: The On-Line Calculation of the AU, Explanatory Note 1
note: Read in full (pdftotext). Prediction constants (solar parallax 8.794142 arcseconds), the per-observation inversion for the AU, the zero-sensitivity sites on the cone-ellipsoid intersection, the linearised coefficient example for the first internal contact, and the constrained solution.

title: Rocher, P. and Arlot, J.-E. (IMCCE) (2004) Analysis of the Observations of Contacts: Calculation of the AU by means of the Entire Data Set, Explanatory Note 2
note: Read in full (pdftotext). Counts per contact, the convergence of the AU as the acceptance window shrinks from 30 to 4 seconds, Tables 1 to 5 including the Delisle pairings, and the explanation of why third-contact timings constrain the AU least.

title: IMCCE for ESO VT-2004, Extended InfoSheet B1: Predictions of the Venus transit of June 8, 2004
note: Read in full (curl). VSOP87, Lieske precession, Wahr nutation, Aoki sidereal time, IAU 1976 constants (solar semidiameter 15'59.63", Venus radius 6051.8 km, Earth radius 6378.140 km), flattening 1/298.257, TT - UTC 65.184 s, general and geocentric phases, the E, F, G coefficients and the Paris example. Formula (1) is an image; its form is reconstructed in the note from the Paris example.

title: IMCCE for ESO VT-2004, Extended InfoSheet B4: An approximate method for calculating the parallax of the Sun
note: Read (curl). The two-site method: the separation of the apparent centres of Venus equals the difference of the parallaxes of Venus and the Sun, and Kepler's third law gives the distance ratio. Numbered formulas are images and were not transcribed.

title: IMCCE for ESO VT-2004, Extended InfoSheet F2: The 1761 transit of Venus
note: Read in full (curl). Delisle's mappemonde, 120 observers at 62 sites, solar parallax results of 8.5 to 10.5 arcseconds, the black drop attributed to diffraction (quoting Couderc and Danjon 1969), and the halo around Venus in 1761.

title: IMCCE for ESO VT-2004, Extended InfoSheet F5: The 1882 transit of Venus
note: Read in full (curl). Expeditions of 1882 and the table of solar parallax determinations from 1761 to the 1990 radar value of 8.79415 arcseconds, including Encke 8.5776 and Newcomb (1890) 8.79 arcseconds.

title: Schneider, G., Pasachoff, J. M. and Golub, L. (2004) TRACE observations of the 15 November 1999 transit of Mercury and the Black Drop effect: considerations for the 2004 transit of Venus. Icarus 168, 249-256
note: Read in full from the uncorrected proof hosted at Williams College (web.williams.edu/Astronomy/eclipse/transits/Icarus_transit.pdf). Black drop seen from space, caused by the instrumental PSF convolved with solar limb darkening; 0.55 arcsecond radius narrowing after deconvolution; 0.56 arcsecond residual edge half-width; diffraction edge of about 43 km at Mercury.

title: Schneider, G., Pasachoff, J. M. and Golub, L. (2003) Space Studies of the Black-Drop Effect at a Mercury Transit. arXiv:astro-ph/0310379 (Highlights of Astronomy 13)
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). Summary of the 1999 and 2003 TRACE analyses, the statement that historical timing accuracy was closer to a minute than a second or two, and that the 2003 data were degraded by compression.

title: Tanga, P., Widemann, T., Sicardy, B., Pasachoff, J. M. et al. (2012) Sunlight refraction in the mesosphere of Venus during the transit on June 8th, 2004. Icarus 218, 207-219 (arXiv:1112.3136)
note: Read the abstract, introduction and model-fit sections from the arXiv PDF, with equations (1) to (4) of the aureole model read in the ar5iv HTML rendering because the PDF text layer drops their symbols. First quantitative photometry of the aureole; fitted scale heights 3.1 and 4.8 km and refracting-layer altitudes 26 and 38.5 km above the reference level at two limb points; apparent Venus radius 28.9 arcseconds.

title: Xie, W., Sigismondi, C., Wang, X. and Tanga, P. (2013) Venus transit, aureole and solar diameter. IAU Symposium 294 proceedings, arXiv:1210.8451
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). The contact-timing method for the solar diameter, the effect of the aureole on contact timings expected at the PSF scale, the Bessel and Gambart 1832 diameters of Mercury, and the lack of time-tagged 2004 ingress and egress image sequences.

title: Emilio, M., Kuhn, J. R., Bush, R. I. and Scholl, I. F. (2012) Measuring the solar radius from space during the 2003 and 2006 Mercury transits. ApJ 750, 135 (arXiv:1203.4898)
note: Read in full from the arXiv PDF, with the radius equation checked against the ar5iv HTML rendering because the PDF text layer drops its symbols. SOHO/MDI contact fitting, the Shapiro (1980) duration relation, the adopted 959.645 arcsecond nominal radius, observed contacts offset 8 s (2003) and 5 s (2006) from the NASA ephemeris, and the 960.12 plus or minus 0.09 arcsecond result.

title: Emilio, M., Bush, R., Kuhn, J. and Scholl, I. (2020) Solar astrometry with planetary transits. Proceedings IAU Symposium 354, 481-490
note: Read in full (Cambridge PDF). Reviews transit radius work: MDI 2003 and 2006 at 960.12 arcseconds, HMI 2012 Venus at 959.57 plus or minus 0.02 arcseconds after PSF correction, a 0.23 arcsecond line-core minus continuum difference, ground scatter of 0.5 to 1 arcsecond per transit, and the claim that the IAU 2015 nominal radius is off by more than 300 km.

title: Sigismondi, C. (2016) The opportunity of the 2016 transit of Mercury for measuring the solar diameter and recommendations for the observation. arXiv:1605.02084
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). Chord-extrapolation method, the 191 s ingress, the 959.63 arcsecond reference, and the estimate that the black drop lasts about 40 seconds after interior contact.

title: Sigismondi, C. and Altafi, H. (2018) Visual and H-alpha measurements of solar diameter of 9 May 2016 Mercury transit. Gerbertvs 11 (arXiv:1805.09915)
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). Observed versus calculated contacts at Rome and Tehran, a radius change of -0.12 plus or minus 0.17 arcseconds, a black drop "confined within 2s", and second-contact delays of 2 to 4 s for most observers.

title: Sigismondi, C., Wang, X., Rocher, P. and Reis-Neto, E. (2013) Venus transits: history and opportunities for planetary, solar and gravitational physics. arXiv:1301.0311
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). Black drop dependence on telescope aperture, the proportion T_calc/T_obs = 959.63"/R, INPOP06 ephemerides for the calculated times, and the shortage of time-tagged 2004 images.

title: Sigismondi, C. (2013) Transits of Venus and the Astronomical Unit: four centuries of increasing precision. arXiv:1301.0296
note: Read in full (arXiv PDF). Horrocks's 1639 observation and estimates, Halley's proposal, and Newcomb's 8.794 plus or minus 0.018 arcsecond solar parallax from the transits.

title: Faherty, J. K., Rodriguez, D. R. and Miller, S. T. (2012) The Hetu'u Global Network: Measuring the Distance to the Sun Using the June 5th/6th Transit of Venus. arXiv:1210.0873
note: Read the method and results sections (arXiv PDF). Delisle's method applied to second and third contacts from school sites, giving 152 plus or minus 30 and 163 plus or minus 30 million km.

title: Sigismondi, C., Bordoni, L. and Pasachoff, J. (2019) Transit of Mercury and General Relativity from Observations, and the 2019 November 11 Transit. Journal for Occultation Astronomy 2019-3, 7-8
note: Read in full (pdftotext). Pre-event plan: lucky imaging, 0.1 s timing for 0.1 arcsecond on the limb, Mercury scanning 10 arcseconds in 100 s, and the observing network. No results.

title: British Astronomical Association Mercury and Venus Section (2020) The 2019 transit of Mercury. Journal of the BAA
note: Read (pdftotext; layout partly garbled). Observer report with BAA Handbook predicted times of 12:35:26 and 18:04:14 UT, no black-drop sightings submitted, and no timing analysis.

title: Jubier, X., Solar Transits pages (index)
note: Read (curl). Links to the 2004, 2006, 2012, 2016 and 2019 transit pages, the Mercury and Venus transit calculators and the Six Millennium Canon of Solar Transits database.

title: Jubier, X., Six Millennium Canon of Solar Transits: -1999 to +4000 (database interface)
note: Read (curl). States 81 Venus transits from -1999 to +4000 and 94 Mercury transits from 1601 to 2300, data provided by Espenak and Meeus, and the ΔT caveat. The page calls the source a NASA Technical Publication without a report number.

title: Jubier, X., MercuryTransitCalculator.js (Mercury transit calculator source)
note: Read in full (curl). Element arrays per transit with t0 and ΔT, Sun 959.62 arcseconds (comment 959.63), Mercury 3.3558 arcseconds (comment 3.3629), solar parallax 8.794142 arcseconds, the topocentric shift formulas, the contact iteration and the flattening factor 0.996647189335.

title: Jubier, X., VenusTransitCalculator.js (Venus transit calculator source)
note: Read (curl). Same structure as the Mercury calculator, Venus 8.3442 arcseconds (comment 8.41), element arrays for 2004 (ΔT 64.184 and 64.635 s) and 2012 (66.76 s).

title: Stellarium, src/gui/AstroCalcDialog.cpp, functions generateTransits, localTransit and TransitBessel::computeElements, commit 69888f4f47af2aa4d1c9d14ec3853e874e253c73
note: Read lines 4523 to 4990 of a local clone at that commit. Besselian elements for transits adapted from the 1961 Supplement, synodic stepping from a reference conjunction, the gamma threshold 0.9972 + L1, the iteration to 0.1 s and the contact corrections.

title: Stellarium, data/ssystem_major.ini (master branch, planet radii)
note: Read (curl of the raw file). Sun 696000 km, Mercury 2440.53 km, Venus 6051.8 km, Earth 6378.1366 km.

title: Swiss Ephemeris, swevents.c, commit 9083a12d59e98034fb2337061481ac8800c16e64
note: Read lines 240 to 250 and 800 to 880 of a local clone at that commit. Lists transit begin, middle and end from minimum elongation and a linear-motion step, with Sun 959.63, Venus 8.34 and Mercury 3.36 arcseconds.

title: Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Ephemeris and the American Ephemeris and Nautical Almanac (1961), section 9F Transits of Mercury, pages 262 to 276
note: Read in full (OCR text). Node condition and the table of node limits, dates and frequencies (Mercury ascending node about 16 November 238 arcminutes, descending 8 May 108; Venus ascending 9 December 37, descending 7 June 41), Newcomb's heliocentric method and the transit fundamental plane, the light-time rule, the contact solution, least distance, position angles with V, Newcomb's q p w, the B C D reduction and Examples 9.26 to 9.32 for 1960 November 7. The node-limit formula for theta and the cone-angle equation are damaged in the OCR text and are not transcribed.

title: Keys, D., Burns, M. and Kercheval, B. (2009) Design and Development of the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) Electrical Power System, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, NTRS 20090027804
note: Read the mission overview (pdftotext). States that SDO operates in an inclined geosynchronous orbit, at an altitude of 35,788 km, longitude 105 degrees W and 28.7 degrees inclination. Used only for the spacecraft's distance from the Earth's centre.

title: Seidelmann, P. K. (ed.), Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac (1992), sections 1.541, 3.257 and 8.5 (transits of Mercury and Venus)
note: The same book as bes-es1992; these are the sections the transit notes quote, read in the archive.org full text: the node condition, the transit counts and the transit section of chapter 8.
